script.opening: "Hiya doc — just ringing about that sugar blood test from my health check. The receptionist said it wasn’t in the diabetes range, so that’s a relief, I dodged it! So I’m fine then, yeah? I’ll just carry on and we recheck it next year or whenever. Cheers for letting me know — I was a bit worried with my dad having had it, but sounds like I’m in the clear."

facts.text: HbA1c 47 is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (pre-diabetes; 42–47), NOT "the clear" — it is a fork in the road. A meaningful proportion progress to type 2 diabetes each year, but progression is PREVENTABLE: intensive lifestyle change (and referral to the Diabetes Prevention Programme) can substantially reduce risk, and some return to normal. "I’m fine" is a missed-opportunity trap.

BMI 33, BP 146/90 (raised), strong family history (father T2DM + early MI), sedentary, poor diet — this is high cardiovascular risk, not just a sugar number. The consultation is an opportunity to address BP (a clinic reading of 146/90 needs ambulatory or home monitoring to confirm hypertension before any treatment decision — NICE NG136), weight, QRISK/lipids (NICE NG238) and lifestyle, not only the HbA1c.

HIDDEN AGENDA — his relief and "leave it" mask genuine FEAR: watching his father decline with diabetes complications and die early frightened him, and "dodging it" lets him not think about it. There’s also a practical barrier (a taxi driver who sits all day, eats on the road, can’t see how to change) and a fatalistic "it got my dad, it’ll get me" undercurrent. Converting relief-avoidance into motivated prevention is the consultation.

If reached: he’d actually be motivated by the goal of NOT following his father’s path — framed as "this is the warning that lets you avoid what happened to your dad", pre-diabetes becomes empowering rather than either ignored or fatalistic.

Officially: confirmation he’s "fine" and can leave it. What he needs: to understand 47 is a modifiable warning (not "the clear"), realistic lifestyle change for a taxi driver, DPP referral, BP/weight/cardiovascular-risk management, a recheck plan, and his father-driven fear turned into motivation.

ice.ideas: Not in the diabetes range = "I’m fine, I dodged it", so he can carry on and recheck next year.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear from watching his father decline and die early with diabetes; "dodging it" lets him avoid thinking about it; a fatalistic "it got my dad, it’ll get me", and a practical sense that a sedentary taxi job makes change impossible.
ice.expectations: Confirmation he’s fine and can leave it. What he actually needs: to grasp that 47 is a modifiable warning, realistic lifestyle change + DPP referral, BP/cardiovascular-risk management, a recheck plan, and his fear turned into motivation.

BMI 33 + BP 146/90 + father T2DM/early MI + sedentary — high cardiovascular risk, not just a sugar number.

checkpoints.text: Reframes HbA1c 47 accurately: NOT "the clear" but non-diabetic hyperglycaemia / pre-diabetes — a modifiable WARNING with real progression risk to type 2 diabetes that lifestyle change can substantially reduce (and sometimes reverse); avoids the "you’re fine, recheck next year" trap

Refers to / recommends the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme (or structured lifestyle support) and gives specific, realistic lifestyle advice (diet, weight loss, physical activity) tailored to a sedentary taxi driver

Treats the WHOLE cardiovascular risk, not just glucose: addresses raised BP (146/90 — NICE NG136: clinic BP 140/90 or more → offer ambulatory, or home, BP monitoring to confirm hypertension before treating), weight, QRISK/lipids and statin discussion (NICE NG238: offer atorvastatin 20 mg if the 10-year QRISK3 risk is 10% or more), smoking status, and family history — recognising this as high CVD risk

Sets a monitoring plan: at least annual HbA1c (NICE PH38; sooner if higher-risk), BP follow-up with ambulatory/home readings, and clear thresholds (HbA1c ≥48 = diabetes) — framing monitoring as part of an active prevention plan, not passive waiting
Converts the father-driven fear into motivation: frames pre-diabetes as the warning that lets him avoid his father’s path, countering fatalism with genuine agency (the trajectory is changeable)
Hears the relief-avoidance and the underlying fear/fatalism, and engages rather than colluding with "I’m fine, leave it"; explores the taxi-driver practical barriers realistically
Motivates without lecturing or shaming: builds the plan around his real day and his goal of not repeating his father’s decline

Safety-nets and follows up: one or two concrete first steps, DPP/structured-support referral, BP and recheck appointments, what symptoms would prompt earlier review, and a follow-up that keeps him engaged — prevention as an active plan

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you rang — and I want to be straight with you, because ‘you’re fine, dodged it’ isn’t quite the full picture. Your number, 47, isn’t diabetes — but it’s not the all-clear either. It’s what we call pre-diabetes: a warning light on the dashboard. The brilliant thing is, a warning light is exactly what you WANT, because it means you can act before the engine trouble — and most people who act don’t go on to develop diabetes."

"You mentioned your dad. Can I be honest? I think watching him go through diabetes is part of why you’d rather not think about this. But here’s the flip: your dad probably never got a warning like this. You have. This is your chance to NOT follow his path — and that’s genuinely in your hands, not just fate."

"And it’s not just the sugar. Your blood pressure’s up a bit and your weight’s carrying some risk too — together those are about your heart as much as diabetes, which matters given your dad’s heart attack. So this is one consultation that can protect a lot at once."

"I’m not going to tell a man who drives all day to ‘go to the gym and cook from scratch’. Let’s be real: swapping the nightly takeaway for something lighter a few nights a week, water instead of fizzy/energy drinks in the cab, a proper walk on your breaks, parking a bit further out. Small, repeatable. And there’s a free NHS prevention programme I’d love to refer you to — it’s practical and made for exactly this."

"So: I’ll refer you to that prevention programme, get your blood pressure checked properly with a 24-hour monitor or a week of home readings, because one reading in a clinic isn’t enough to decide, look at your heart risk and whether a statin would help, and we’ll repeat the sugar in a few months — not ‘next year and forget it’. If it ever hit 48, that’s the diabetes line, but the whole point is to push it the OTHER way. Most people can."

"Pick ONE thing to start this week — say, the cab drinks — and we build from there. If you get the classic diabetes symptoms meanwhile — really thirsty, weeing loads, weight dropping — ring sooner. Come and see me to set this up properly. You called thinking you were in the clear; what you’ve actually got is the best kind of warning — one you can still do something about."

f.learning: An HbA1c of 47 mmol/mol is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (pre-diabetes), NOT "the all-clear" — it is a modifiable fork in the road with real progression risk to type 2 diabetes that intensive lifestyle change can substantially reduce (and sometimes reverse). The trap is the relief-driven "I’m fine, leave it, recheck next year"; the task is to reframe it as a warning that can be acted on, refer to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme with realistic lifestyle advice tailored to the patient’s actual life (here a sedentary taxi driver), and treat the WHOLE cardiometabolic risk — raised BP (146/90, confirmed by ambulatory or home monitoring before treatment — NICE NG136), weight, QRISK/lipids (NICE NG238), family history — not just the glucose number, with an active monitoring plan (NICE PH38: at least annual HbA1c; BP follow-up; the 48 = diabetes threshold). The examinable hidden agenda is that the relief masks fear and fatalism from watching his father decline and die early with diabetes; convert that into motivation ("this is the warning that lets you avoid his path"), build the plan around his real day without lecturing, and safety-net hyperglycaemic symptoms. Prevention framed as agency, not passive waiting.

knowledge.guideline: NICE PH38 (type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk) · NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme · NICE NG136 · NICE NG238
knowledge.summary: An HbA1c of 47 mmol/mol is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia: high risk, not “the clear”. Refer to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme and deal with the whole cardiovascular risk, not just the sugar.

points.t: HbA1c 42–47 mmol/mol (or fasting glucose 5.5–6.9 mmol/L) = non-diabetic hyperglycaemia, a high risk of type 2 diabetes (NICE PH38). 48 mmol/mol or above is the diagnostic threshold for diabetes (WHO 2011, international).

Refer to an intensive lifestyle-change programme — in England the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme, which has face-to-face, remote and digital options. Weight loss, dietary change and activity (at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, UK Chief Medical Officers’ guidelines 2019) reduce progression.
NICE PH38: offer a blood test (HbA1c or fasting glucose) at least once a year. Frame it as part of an active plan, with a clear route back if he develops symptoms.

NICE PH38: consider metformin, using clinical judgement, when HbA1c or fasting glucose is getting worse despite (or he cannot take part in) an intensive lifestyle programme, particularly with a BMI over 35. Not first-line here.
Clinic BP of 140/90 or above: offer ambulatory (or home) monitoring to confirm hypertension before treating (NICE NG136). A single reading of 146/90 needs confirming, not ignoring.

Calculate QRISK3 once lipids are available; NICE NG238 recommends offering atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention when the 10-year risk is 10% or more. A father with an early heart attack makes a formal risk assessment essential.

model.text: Hello, is that Mr Grant? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I just check your date of birth? … Thank you. Is now a good time to talk for ten minutes or so — are you somewhere you can speak, not driving?
model.why: Identity check and safe setting for a telephone consultation with a driver

model.text: Yeah, I’m parked up. The receptionist said my sugar test wasn’t in the diabetes range, so I dodged it! I’m fine then, yeah? We’ll just recheck next year.

I’m really glad you rang, and I can hear the relief. You’re right that it isn’t diabetes. I’d like to explain what the number does mean, because it’s actually useful news. Before that, can I ask a bit about you, so the advice fits your life?
model.why: Acknowledges the relief without colluding; sets the agenda

model.text: Go on then.
You mentioned being a bit worried because of your dad. What happened with him?
model.why: Picks up the cue in his opening call

model.text: He had type 2 diabetes. He went downhill with it, had a heart attack young, and he died early. I watched all that.
I’m sorry. That’s a hard thing to have watched. Thank you for telling me. Tell me about a typical working day — hours, food, getting about.
model.why: Empathic response, then an open question on context

model.text: Long shifts in the cab. Sat down all day, eating on the road. Takeaway most nights because I’m shattered when I get in.
That’s honest, thank you. Any thirst, passing a lot of urine, weight loss, or infections that keep coming back?
No, nothing like that.
And do you smoke, or have you had your cholesterol result from the health check?
The nurse went through all that on the form. I don’t remember the cholesterol number.
No problem, I’ll look it up from the health check record.
model.why: Keeps the data neutral and follows up the missing information

model.text: When the receptionist said it wasn’t diabetes, what went through your mind?
model.why: Explores the meaning behind “I dodged it”

model.text: Relief. Honestly, I try not to think about it. It got my dad, and part of me thinks it’ll get me in the end whatever I do.
That makes sense after what you saw, and I’m glad you said it, because I don’t think that’s true for you. What would you like to get from this call?
model.why: Names the fatalism and elicits expectations

model.text: Just to know I’m okay, really.

Here’s the straight answer. 47 isn’t diabetes — diabetes starts at 48. But it isn’t the all-clear either. It’s what we call pre-diabetes: a warning light on the dashboard. It means a higher chance of diabetes, and the good news is that this is exactly the stage where you can change the outcome.
model.why: Accurate reframe: non-diabetic hyperglycaemia, not “the clear”

model.text: So I haven’t dodged it.
Not yet — but you’ve been given the warning. Your dad may never have had one. You have, and what you do next can keep you off his path. That’s in your hands.
model.why: Turns the father’s story into motivation

model.text: (pause) I hadn’t thought of it like that.
And it isn’t just the sugar. Your blood pressure was a bit high at the check, and your weight adds to the risk. With your dad’s heart attack, I want to look at your heart risk as a whole.
model.why: Whole cardiovascular risk, not just glucose

model.text: There’s a free NHS diabetes prevention programme — practical support with food and activity, and you can do it in person, remotely or on an app, which might suit shifts. Would you like me to refer you?
model.why: NHS DPP referral tailored to his work pattern

model.text: An app I could do on breaks. Go on.
Great. I’m not going to tell a man who drives all day to join a gym. What’s one change you could actually make this week?
Cut the takeaways down to a few nights a week. And maybe walk on my break instead of sitting in the car.

Both good. I’d also like you to borrow a blood-pressure monitor and take readings at home for a week, so we know the real number, and I’ll work out your heart-risk score from your health-check bloods. If it’s 10% or more we’ll talk about a statin. And we’ll recheck your sugar within the year — sooner if you’re worried.
model.why: Confirms BP with HBPM, QRISK3 with statin threshold, and HbA1c monitoring

model.text: Fair enough. I’m not in trouble with my taxi licence, am I?
No — pre-diabetes doesn’t affect your licence. Getting your blood pressure and sugar under control is also the best way to protect your licence in future.
If you notice real thirst, passing lots of urine, or losing weight without trying, ring us sooner, because that can mean the sugar has gone up. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
Prevention programme on the app, fewer takeaways, walk on breaks, home blood pressure for a week, you check my heart risk, sugar again within the year.
Spot on. I’ll book you in with the home readings in a couple of weeks. You rang thinking you were in the clear — you’ve actually got the best kind of warning, one you can act on. Anything else?
model.why: Summarises, books follow-up and closes on agency

model.text: No. Cheers, doc. Better that than finding out the hard way.

social.t: Long sedentary shifts and meals on the road. Advice must fit the cab: walking on breaks, healthier options on the road, swaps for the nightly takeaway.
Watching his father decline and die early makes him avoid the subject. Fatalism predicts disengagement, so address it directly.

legal.t: Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia doesn’t need to be reported. Taxi licensing authorities commonly apply DVLA Group 2 standards; Group 2 drivers are disqualified if resting BP is consistently 180 systolic or more, or 100 diastolic or more. If diabetes develops later, some treatments (such as sulfonylureas or insulin) carry reporting duties — check DVLA guidance then.

professional.t: The receptionist’s “not diabetes” was accurate but incomplete. Results in a risk range need a clinician’s explanation; consider how the practice relays borderline results.
Offer DPP referral, home BP and a statin discussion as choices he makes, and record his decisions.

community.t: NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme (including digital options), NHS Health Check follow-up, community pharmacy BP checks, and Diabetes UK information on reducing risk.

playbook.diagnosis: Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (HbA1c 47 mmol/mol) in a man with obesity, a raised clinic BP to be confirmed, and a family history of type 2 diabetes and early MI — high risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of 47 as an orange warning light on the dashboard. The engine hasn’t broken down — that would be diabetes, at 48 — but the light tells you now, while you can still do something about it.”

management.reflectIce: “You said it got your dad and you think it’ll get you. The difference is you’ve had the warning he never got — and that means you can take a different road.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around cab shifts: fewer takeaways, walks on breaks, the DPP app; agree one change he chooses.
sharedPlan: Refer to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme (digital option)
Home BP for a week to confirm or exclude hypertension (NICE NG136)
QRISK3 from the health-check lipids; offer atorvastatin 20 mg if 10% or more (NICE NG238); HbA1c at least annually (NICE PH38)
safetyNet: Thirst, polyuria or weight loss — ring sooner for an earlier HbA1c
BP review with home readings in two weeks; chest pain or severe headache — urgent help

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station looks easy because the result isn’t diabetes. It is failed by agreeing with him, by lecturing, and by treating the sugar in isolation from his blood pressure and family history.

items.fail: “Good news, it’s not diabetes. We’ll repeat it in a year.”
items.why: HbA1c 47 is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia; NICE PH38 expects referral to an intensive lifestyle programme, not passive rechecking.
items.fix: Reframe it as a warning light and refer to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme.

items.fail: Discussing only glucose and missing the BP of 146/90 and the father’s early MI.
items.why: His cardiovascular risk is the bigger picture; missing it is “management plan incomplete”.
items.fix: Home BP to confirm (NICE NG136), QRISK3 with a statin discussion if 10% or more (NICE NG238).

items.fail: Hearing “it got my dad” and moving straight to diet advice.
items.why: The fatalism is what stops him changing. Ignoring the cue loses the Relating marks.
items.fix: “Your dad may never have had a warning. You have — and that’s in your hands.”

items.fail: Prescribing an idealised lifestyle: gym, home cooking, 150 minutes a week.
items.why: It ignores long cab shifts and invites quiet disengagement.
items.fix: Ask for one change he will make this week, and offer the DPP digital route that fits breaks.

items.fail: Starting a telephone consultation with a taxi driver without checking he isn’t driving.
items.why: Safety and confidentiality on the phone are part of Global Skills.
items.fix: “Are you somewhere you can talk — not driving?”

items.fail: Ending with “any questions?” and no follow-up booked.
items.why: No safety-net and no confirmed plan are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Teach-back, BP review with home readings in two weeks, and symptoms that mean ringing sooner.

SCA_MODELS.why: NHS DPP referral tailored to his work pattern

SCA_MODELS.text: An app I could do on breaks. Go on.
Great. I’m not going to tell a man who drives all day to join a gym. What’s one change you could actually make this week?
Cut the takeaways down to a few nights a week. And maybe walk on my break instead of sitting in the car.

Both good. I’d also like you to borrow a blood-pressure monitor and take readings at home for a week, so we know the real number, and I’ll work out your heart-risk score from your health-check bloods. If it’s 10% or more we’ll talk about a statin. And we’ll recheck your sugar within the year — sooner if you’re worried.
SCA_MODELS.why: Confirms BP with HBPM, QRISK3 with statin threshold, and HbA1c monitoring

SCA_MODELS.text: Fair enough. I’m not in trouble with my taxi licence, am I?
No — pre-diabetes doesn’t affect your licence. Getting your blood pressure and sugar under control is also the best way to protect your licence in future.
If you notice real thirst, passing lots of urine, or losing weight without trying, ring us sooner, because that can mean the sugar has gone up. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
Prevention programme on the app, fewer takeaways, walk on breaks, home blood pressure for a week, you check my heart risk, sugar again within the year.
Spot on. I’ll book you in with the home readings in a couple of weeks. You rang thinking you were in the clear — you’ve actually got the best kind of warning, one you can act on. Anything else?
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises, books follow-up and closes on agency

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Cheers, doc. Better that than finding out the hard way.

SCA_STEM.name: Wesley Grant
pmh: Family history: father — type 2 diabetes and an early heart attack
SCA_STEM.recent: NHS Health Check: HbA1c 47 mmol/mol. BMI 33. BP 146/90. Occupation: taxi driver.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call about his health-check blood result.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE PH38 (type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk) · NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme · NICE NG136 · NICE NG238
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: An HbA1c of 47 mmol/mol is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia: high risk, not “the clear”. Refer to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme and deal with the whole cardiovascular risk, not just the sugar.

points.t: HbA1c 42–47 mmol/mol (or fasting glucose 5.5–6.9 mmol/L) = non-diabetic hyperglycaemia, a high risk of type 2 diabetes (NICE PH38). 48 mmol/mol or above is the diagnostic threshold for diabetes (WHO 2011, international).

Refer to an intensive lifestyle-change programme — in England the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme, which has face-to-face, remote and digital options. Weight loss, dietary change and activity (at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, UK Chief Medical Officers’ guidelines 2019) reduce progression.
NICE PH38: offer a blood test (HbA1c or fasting glucose) at least once a year. Frame it as part of an active plan, with a clear route back if he develops symptoms.

NICE PH38: consider metformin, using clinical judgement, when HbA1c or fasting glucose is getting worse despite (or he cannot take part in) an intensive lifestyle programme, particularly with a BMI over 35. Not first-line here.
Clinic BP of 140/90 or above: offer ambulatory (or home) monitoring to confirm hypertension before treating (NICE NG136). A single reading of 146/90 needs confirming, not ignoring.

Calculate QRISK3 once lipids are available; NICE NG238 recommends offering atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention when the 10-year risk is 10% or more. A father with an early heart attack makes a formal risk assessment essential.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him say “I dodged it, I’m fine” in full; confirmed a safe place to talk (not driving).
Long cab shifts, eating on the road, takeaways most nights, sitting all day; how his work shapes what change is realistic.
Picked up the passing mention of his father and the fatalism behind “it’ll get me in the end”.
Idea (not diabetes means fine); concern (his father’s decline and early death); expectation (to be told he’s okay and can recheck next year).
Home or ambulatory BP; QRISK3 from health-check lipids; HbA1c at least annually; smoking status from the record.
Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia versus undiagnosed diabetes (symptom screen); hypertension to confirm; high cardiovascular risk.
Screened for osmotic symptoms and weight loss; recognised cardiovascular risk from the family history of early MI.
HbA1c 47 = non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (NICE PH38): high risk, not “the clear”.
NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme referral (digital option for shifts); one negotiated goal; HBPM; statin discussion if QRISK3 ≥10%.
Addressed BP and weight alongside glucose; metformin not first-line (NICE PH38).
Annual HbA1c; BP review in two weeks; safety-net for thirst, polyuria and weight loss; licence question answered.

social.t: Long sedentary shifts and meals on the road. Advice must fit the cab: walking on breaks, healthier options on the road, swaps for the nightly takeaway.
Watching his father decline and die early makes him avoid the subject. Fatalism predicts disengagement, so address it directly.

legal.t: Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia doesn’t need to be reported. Taxi licensing authorities commonly apply DVLA Group 2 standards; Group 2 drivers are disqualified if resting BP is consistently 180 systolic or more, or 100 diastolic or more. If diabetes develops later, some treatments (such as sulfonylureas or insulin) carry reporting duties — check DVLA guidance then.

professional.t: The receptionist’s “not diabetes” was accurate but incomplete. Results in a risk range need a clinician’s explanation; consider how the practice relays borderline results.
Offer DPP referral, home BP and a statin discussion as choices he makes, and record his decisions.

community.t: NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme (including digital options), NHS Health Check follow-up, community pharmacy BP checks, and Diabetes UK information on reducing risk.

redFlags: Thirst, polyuria, unintended weight loss or recurrent infections — possible diabetes needing earlier testing
Chest pain or breathlessness on exertion — his cardiovascular risk is high
Very high BP (180/120 or above) with symptoms — same-day assessment
psychosocial: Long sedentary cab shifts, eating on the road, takeaways most nights
His father’s decline, early heart attack and death
Fatalism: “it’ll get me in the end whatever I do”
ice: Idea: “It’s not diabetes, so I dodged it — I’m fine”
Concern: ending up like his father (unspoken at first)
Expectation: to be told he’s okay and recheck next year

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (HbA1c 47 mmol/mol) in a man with obesity, a raised clinic BP to be confirmed, and a family history of type 2 diabetes and early MI — high risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of 47 as an orange warning light on the dashboard. The engine hasn’t broken down — that would be diabetes, at 48 — but the light tells you now, while you can still do something about it.”

management.reflectIce: “You said it got your dad and you think it’ll get you. The difference is you’ve had the warning he never got — and that means you can take a different road.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around cab shifts: fewer takeaways, walks on breaks, the DPP app; agree one change he chooses.
sharedPlan: Refer to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme (digital option)
Home BP for a week to confirm or exclude hypertension (NICE NG136)
QRISK3 from the health-check lipids; offer atorvastatin 20 mg if 10% or more (NICE NG238); HbA1c at least annually (NICE PH38)
safetyNet: Thirst, polyuria or weight loss — ring sooner for an earlier HbA1c
BP review with home readings in two weeks; chest pain or severe headache — urgent help

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station looks easy because the result isn’t diabetes. It is failed by agreeing with him, by lecturing, and by treating the sugar in isolation from his blood pressure and family history.

items.fail: “Good news, it’s not diabetes. We’ll repeat it in a year.”
items.why: HbA1c 47 is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia; NICE PH38 expects referral to an intensive lifestyle programme, not passive rechecking.
items.fix: Reframe it as a warning light and refer to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme.

items.fail: Discussing only glucose and missing the BP of 146/90 and the father’s early MI.
items.why: His cardiovascular risk is the bigger picture; missing it is “management plan incomplete”.
items.fix: Home BP to confirm (NICE NG136), QRISK3 with a statin discussion if 10% or more (NICE NG238).

items.fail: Hearing “it got my dad” and moving straight to diet advice.
items.why: The fatalism is what stops him changing. Ignoring the cue loses the Relating marks.
items.fix: “Your dad may never have had a warning. You have — and that’s in your hands.”

items.fail: Prescribing an idealised lifestyle: gym, home cooking, 150 minutes a week.
items.why: It ignores long cab shifts and invites quiet disengagement.
items.fix: Ask for one change he will make this week, and offer the DPP digital route that fits breaks.

items.fail: Starting a telephone consultation with a taxi driver without checking he isn’t driving.
items.why: Safety and confidentiality on the phone are part of Global Skills.
items.fix: “Are you somewhere you can talk — not driving?”

items.fail: Ending with “any questions?” and no follow-up booked.
items.why: No safety-net and no confirmed plan are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Teach-back, BP review with home readings in two weeks, and symptoms that mean ringing sooner.
